---
title: |
  Reported Attachment, Revealed Discrimination: What the Party-Closeness Item Selects On in Europe
abstract: |
  Affective polarization is estimated on partisans, so someone must decide who counts as one. In Europe that decision usually rests on a single self-report -- whether a respondent says they feel close to a party -- an item whose prevalence ranges from roughly 41% to 85% across countries. We hold the partisan anchor constant and vary only the reporting: self-identified partisans are compared against vote-anchored respondents who deny feeling close to any party, using thermometer ratings and conjoint trust and dictator games from 25 European democracies (N = 22,858). Both groups favor co-partisans strongly in the games, and by indistinguishable amounts; the same respondents differ substantially in party-directed animus on the thermometers. Self-reported attachment inflates measured polarization without corresponding to any additional discrimination in behavior. It behaves like a reporting disposition, not an identity.

## Introduction {#sec-intro}

**Purpose**

- State the central claim in the first paragraph, before any literature.
- Name what it contradicts: standard coding practice in comparative AP research, and the identity/expressive-partisanship account of what attachment does.
- Establish that "who counts as a partisan" is a consequential measurement choice, not a technical footnote.
- Set up the two empirical claims (§3 coding practice, §6 the behavioral null) as the contribution.

**What must hold**

- The claim is stated as *attitudinal vs. behavioral*, never vertical vs. horizontal.
- The magnitude of the co-partisan effect (β₁) is previewed *before* the reader is told it does not vary by type (β₃) -- otherwise the null reads as "nothing happens".
- The contribution is framed as measurement, not as adjudicating identity vs. categorization; the theory payoff is ceilinged in §9.
- "Vote-anchored" throughout; never "leaners", never "implicit partisans" in prose.

## What attachment measures in Europe {#sec-attachment}

**Purpose**

- Makes step 2 of the chain: the attachment item does not cleanly identify partisans in Europe. Without this the paper is a null result about nothing.
- Fixes the taxonomy used everywhere after: self-identified partisans / vote-anchored respondents / non-partisans.
- Draws the key distinction: attachment used as a *binary selection filter* vs. attachment as a *graded identity measure*. The paper's target is the former.
- Engages Bankert/Huddy expressive partisanship as the strongest counter-position, on its own terms.

**What must hold**

- Converse & Dupeux and Thomassen carry the conceptual point: in Europe the attachment report follows the vote rather than preceding it.
- The cross-national spread in attachment shares is *shown*, not asserted (~41% LV to ~85% DK) -- @fig-impl-expl-distribution below; long-run decline from the Mannheim Trend File / CSES if it earns its space.
- 3--4 pages, not a review. Anything not bearing on "filter or identity?" is cut.
- Vote-anchored ≠ leaners is stated here as terminology; the empirical overlap estimate is deferred to §4.
- Figure: the taxonomy itself (PIDs / vote-anchored / non-partisans), showing what each coding rule keeps and drops.

## Coding practice in comparative AP research {#sec-coding-practice}

::: {.callout-note}
EMPIRICAL CLAIM 1.
:::

**Purpose**

- Shows the field actually makes this choice, and mostly makes it silently -- so the problem is the literature's, not a hypothetical the paper invented.
- Converts step 3 into something a reader can check: which papers, which rule, what they say about the respondents they drop.

**What must hold**

- A **census**, not a sample, of comparative/European AP articles in a named journal set over defined years. *(Open decision: journal set and year range -- Tristan to specify.)* Target ~40 papers.
- Hand-coded on **two dimensions only**: ingroup criterion, non-identifier treatment. Resisting scope creep here is what keeps the section credible.
- Coding rules stated so a reader could reproduce them; ambiguous and unclear cases reported rather than resolved by inference.
- Expected pattern: silent exclusion dominates, and mode is confounded with definition at the field level (behavioral studies anchor on vote, attitudinal on attachment). If the pattern does not appear, the section still stands as description -- say so.
- Out of scope: the LLM literature-classification pipeline. That is a separate paper; nothing from it feeds this section.

## Design: holding the anchor constant {#sec-design}

**Purpose**

- Makes step 5 credible: the two groups differ in whether attachment is *reported*, not in whether they have a party.
- This is the section referees will attack. Every assumption gets named here and answered here, not in limitations.

**What must hold**

- Data and sample construction: `eu25games2019` harmonized release; attention check, completion, games played, earliest game wave per panelist; 22,858 respondents × 6 rounds. Sample decisions are this project's own, so they must be defended, not inherited.
- Anchor construction: attachment party for self-identified partisans, recall-maximizing vote anchor for vote-anchored respondents; non-partisans have no defensible anchor and are excluded from contrasts requiring one.
- The linear predictor and what each coefficient means: β₁ = co-partisan effect, β₃ = its difference by type. Estimand stated explicitly.
- **Comparability.** Party-within-country varying intercepts and slopes, so the contrast is estimated inside party-country cells. Report balance. State plainly: this rules out composition, it does **not** identify a causal effect.
- **Defectors** (attachment party ≠ vote party) are otherwise assigned an anchor by fiat. Code both anchors and test which predicts ratings and allocations.
- **Leaner overlap** estimated from the CSES branching probe -- the only source carrying it. Report the overlap; do not assume the groups are distinct.
- **The design confound, stated here.** Target and measurement mode are perfectly confounded in these data: thermometers are vertical-attitudinal, the conjoint horizontal-behavioral, the diagonal is unobserved. The claim is therefore attitudinal vs. behavioral, full stop.
- **The equivalence test is pre-specified here, before results.** ROPE in token units, justified against the size of β₁. Committing to it after seeing the posterior is worthless.

## Attitudinal result {#sec-attitudinal}

**Purpose**

- The *contrast case*, not the finding: establishes that there is a large, consistent gap to be explained, which §6 then fails to find in behavior.
- Absorbs country heterogeneity -- one figure here, not a separate section.

**What must hold**

- Concede up front that the attachment item and the thermometer are partly mechanically related; a reader who spots this before the paper does will discount the rest.
- The gap must hold *inside* party-country cells, not only pooled -- otherwise it is composition.
- Consistency across the 25 countries shown once, with the magnitude variation described rather than modelled a second time.
- Framing discipline: this section is a benchmark for §6. It is not the headline.

## Behavioral result {#sec-behavioral}

::: {.callout-note}
EMPIRICAL CLAIM 2. The load-bearing section.
:::

**Purpose**

- Establishes that the discrimination is there in both groups and does not differ by type -- the empirical core of step 6, and the whole basis for step 7.

**What must hold**

- **Order is not negotiable.** Report the magnitude of β₁ first: both partisan types favor co-partisans substantially and credibly. Only then report β₃ ≈ 0.
- The null is *tested*, not inferred: posterior mass inside the pre-specified ROPE. Overlapping credible intervals are not evidence of equivalence and must not be presented as such.
- Answer "your null reflects weak design" twice over: β₁ itself shows the instrument has power, and the partisan attribute is benchmarked against EU position, class, and religion within the same conjoint.
- Country-level results shown to be consistent with the pooled estimate, without turning into a second heterogeneity section.
- The vertical/horizontal 2×2 survives here and only here, as a conceptual device explaining why the answer splits by measure. It is not the paper's framing.

## Does attachment do work, or mark prior investment? {#sec-panel}

**Purpose**

- Main text, not appendix. Without it, "attachment is just a report" and "attachment marks something real that the games cannot see" both survive §6.
- Tests within person whether acquiring or losing attachment changes anything, using external panel data.

**What must hold**

- **Gate, checked before the section is written:** the attachment transition matrix must show real within-person movement. If it is thin, drop the section rather than report an underpowered result.
- One country, one panel, done properly -- see the candidate list in `data/01_raw/external-data.md`. Exactly one gets downloaded.
- Cross-source comparability caveats stated: different instrument, different context, not a replication of the games.
- Ceiling stated explicitly: the design cannot separate attachment *creating* investment from *marking* it.

## What this does to comparative estimates {#sec-comparative}

**Purpose**

- Calibration: turns the finding into the quantity a comparative researcher actually faces when choosing a coding rule.

**What must hold**

- All four ingroup codings re-estimated on the same data: identity only; recall-maximizing (attachment, else vote); vote only; most-liked party.
- Country rank correlations reported alongside level differences -- committed in advance to reporting either way. If ranks are ~0.95, the deflationary result is still the result and still a contribution.
- Note that most-liked-party coding selects on the outcome and is mechanically inflationary; it is included as a comparison, not as a candidate rule.

## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

**Purpose**

- Measurement implication first: what a comparative researcher should do differently when coding partisans, and what published cross-national AP levels partly reflect.
- Theory implication second and ceilinged.
- Limitations owned in the text, not deflected to a list.

**What must hold**

- Measurement: cross-national differences in AP levels partly reflect national differences in willingness to say "close to", not only differences in polarization.
- Theory: the pattern fits categorization sufficiency in the behavioral domain, but the design cannot adjudicate identity vs. categorization. Say so before a referee does.
- Limitations conceded before they are raised: ten hypothetical tokens may not be where identity shows up; a single 2019 cross-section speaks to level, not trend; the conjoint labels identities that real encounters only cue; the attitudinal measures are party-targeted only.

### Survey item wording (English version) {.appendix}

| Variable | Question |
|:---|:--------------|
|  Party Attachement | Do you consider yourself to be close to any particular political party? If so, which party do you feel close to? |
|  Vote Intention | Which party will you give your 1st preference vote in this [2019 European] election? |
|  Vote Choice | Which party did you give your 1st preference vote to in this [2019 European] election? |
|  Feeling Thermometer |  We would like to get your feelings toward some political parties and political leaders in the news these days. Below there is a list of parties and people. I'd like you to rate them using something we call the feeling thermometer. Ratings between 50 degrees and 100 degrees mean that you feel favorable and warm toward the party or person. Ratings between 0 degrees and 50 degrees mean that you don't feel favorable toward the party or person and that you don't care too much for that party or person. You would rate the political party or the person at the 50 degree mark if you don't feel particularly warm or cold toward the person. |
: Survey item wording (English version) {#tbl-survey-items}

### Experimental setup {.appendix}

Before the behavioral games, @hahm2024divided presented respondents a short background information overview and instructions. For the dictator game, these were: *This game is played by pairs of individuals.* *Each pair is made up of a Player 1 and a Player 2.* *Each player will have some information about the other player, but you will not be told who the other players are during or after the experiment.* *The game is conducted as follows: A sum of 10 tokens will be provisionally allocated to Player 1 at the start of each round.* *Player 1 will then decide how much of the 10 tokens to offer to Player 2.* *Player 1 could give some, all, or none of the 10 tokens.* *Player 1 keeps all tokens not given to Player 2.* *Player 2 gets to keep all the tokens Player 1 offers.* *You will play this game three times with three different people.* In the trust game, the provided information and instruction were: *This game is played by pairs of individuals.* *Each pair is made up of a Player 1 and a Player 2.* *Each player will have some information about the other player, but you will not be told who the other players are during or after the experiment.* *Each player will receive 10 tokens.* *Player 1 then has the opportunity to give a portion of his or her 10 tokens to Player 2.* *Player 1 could give some, all, or none of the 10 tokens.* *Whatever amount Player 1 decides to give to Player 2 will be tripled before it is passed on to Player 2.* *Player 2 then has the option of returning any portion of this tripled amount to Player 1.* *Then, the game is over.* *Player 1 receives whatever he or she keeps from the original 10 tokens, plus anything returned to him or her by Player 2. Player 2 receives their original 10 tokens, plus whatever he or she keeps after returning any portion of the tripled amount to Player 1.* *You will play this game three times, with three different people.* *The more tokens you obtain, the more successful you will be.*

In both games respondents were shown a tabular overview of Player 2 after the instructions. @fig-example-profile shows an example of such a profile along with the interface respondents were provided to assign the 10 tokens. Each round, a new profile was displayed to respondents.

![Example of potential co-player profile.](images/cj-example-profile.png){#fig-example-profile}

### Robustness {.appendix}

- Attention check switched off (`apply_attention_check`), to show the sample rule does not drive the contrast.
- Defector anchor coded both ways (§4), reported separately for ratings and allocations.
- Response-style check: endpoint use on non-political 0--10 batteries, testing whether the attitudinal gap is partly a scale-use disposition.
